introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections » (3 sections : A 1800-1922, B 1922-1961, C 1961 to present, 4 questions chacune). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé, une règle `parmi 1 sur 4` par section ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « (25 marks) » et la page de garde dit « All questions carry equal marks » ; `points` de l'exercice et de la question unique valent 25. Aucun écart avec le sujet (4 x 25 = 100).

Défauts d'impression du sujet : la page de garde est coupée au bord droit (« All th[e] questions carry equal marks », le mot « the » est tronqué) ; la question 6 se termine par « after 1945?. » (point d'interrogation suivi d'un point). La question 6 est transcrite avec un seul point d'interrogation. Sujet scanné (deux pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure, carte ni document. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, History 2, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, code 0760, JUNE 2023.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les dates, noms et traités sont ceux de l'historiographie établie ; les faits dont la précision est moindre sont formulés prudemment ou sans chiffre.

Question 1 (migrations des Grassfields) : les dates et l'ordre exact des migrations (installation des Bali-Chamba sous Fonyonga I, arrivée des groupes Widikum, expansion bamoum) sont donnés seulement à l'échelle de la première moitié du XIXe siècle ; les traditions orales divergent et aucune date précise n'est avancée.

Question 2 : les dates 1843 (Merrick à Fernando Po, 1844 à Bimbia), 1844 (Saker à Fernando Po), 1845 (Bethel, Douala), 1858 (Victoria), 1872 (Bible en duala), 1880 (mort de Saker) et 1886 (passage à la Mission de Bâle) sont celles de l'historiographie courante ; les traités anti-esclavagistes de 1840 avec Bell et Akwa et les lettres des chefs duala à la reine Victoria (fin des années 1870 et début des années 1880) sont cités sans détail.

Question 4 : les dates de la campagne (Douala 27 septembre 1914, Garoua juin 1915, Yaoundé 1er janvier 1916, Banyo et Mora février 1916) sont celles de l'historiographie courante ; la composition exacte et les effectifs des forces ne sont pas donnés. L'exécution de Rudolf Duala Manga Bell (août 1914) est mentionnée sans détail.

Question 5 : l'ordre en conseil de 1923 et les détails de l'organisation administrative (provinces puis région de l'Est) sont donnés dans leurs grandes lignes, sans date de réforme précise ; l'article 9 du mandat est paraphrasé.

Question 7 : le déroulement exact de la crise de la Région de l'Est en 1953 (querelle interne du NCNC entre Azikiwe et Eyo Ita, retrait des représentants du Southern Cameroons conduits par Endeley de la Chambre d'Enugu, conférences de Londres 1953 et de Lagos 1954) est résumé de mémoire et pourrait comporter des imprécisions de détail ; aucun chiffre de sièges n'est avancé. Les dates de la Constitution de 1954 (statut quasi fédéral) et de l'autonomie complète de 1958 sont données dans leurs grandes lignes.

Question 9 : les résultats chiffrés du plébiscite du 11 février 1961 ne sont pas donnés ; les attributions de la Constitution fédérale (compétences fédérales, article de révision exigeant une majorité des députés du Cameroun occidental) sont résumées sans numéro d'article.

Question 10 : question la moins sûre du sujet. Les circonstances précises de la nomination d'A.N. Jua (1965) et de son remplacement par S.T. Muna (1968) sont mal documentées ; le corrigé donne les raisons habituellement avancées (cumul des fonctions de Foncha, influence d'Ahidjo, rivalités au sein du KNDP, fusion dans l'UNC en 1966, tensions sur les compétences de l'État fédéré, critiques contre l'administration de Jua) en le disant, sans date précise ni fait invérifiable. À faire relire par un historien du Cameroun avant diffusion.

Question 11 : les dates des projets (SONARA 1981, barrage de Song Loulou vers 1981, Lagdo début des années 1980, transcamerounais jusqu'à Ngaoundéré 1974, FONADER 1973, ONCPB 1976-1977, SNH 1980, démission d'Ahidjo le 4 novembre 1982) sont celles de l'historiographie courante ; aucun chiffre de croissance ou de production n'est donné.

Question 12 : les dates (dévaluation du franc CFA le 12 janvier 1994, point de décision de l'initiative PPTE en 2000 et point d'achèvement en 2006, SDF en mai 1990, loi sur le multipartisme en décembre 1990, villes mortes en 1991, Constitution de 1996, opération Épervier en 2006) sont celles de l'historiographie courante ; l'ampleur exacte des baisses de salaires de 1993 n'est pas chiffrée.

questions.enonce_markdown:
To what extent did the Federal Constitution reflect the aspirations of Southern Cameroonians?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** On 11 February 1961 the Southern Cameroons voted in a UN-supervised plebiscite to join the Republic of Cameroon rather than Nigeria (the Northern Cameroons voted to join Nigeria). Before the union, the leaders of the Southern Cameroons (Prime Minister John Ngu Foncha of the KNDP, with the opposition leader Dr Endeley and others) and of the Republic (President Ahmadou Ahidjo) met at the Foumban Conference (17-21 July 1961) to discuss the form of the union. A Federal Constitution was adopted, effective on 1 October 1961, creating the Federal Republic of Cameroon made of two states, East Cameroon and West Cameroon. The question asks how far this Constitution met the hopes of the Southern Cameroonians.

**1. The aspirations of Southern Cameroonians.** The Southern Cameroons' leaders, especially Foncha and the KNDP, wanted reunification but in a form that would (i) keep their identity and their inherited British institutions (English language, common law, the system of education, a House of Chiefs and an independent judiciary); (ii) give them a real share in power as equal partners and not as a minority joined to a larger state; (iii) protect them against domination by the more populous East (several times as large); and (iv) ensure autonomy, with their own government and legislature. At the All-Party Conference in Bamenda (June 1961) they agreed on a federal formula with strong state powers.

**2. Ways in which the Federal Constitution reflected these aspirations.**
*a) Federal structure.* The choice of a federation with two federated states, each with its own government, Prime Minister and legislature (the West Cameroon House of Assembly and a House of Chiefs), was a major demand of the Southern Cameroonians and was met.
*b) Bilingualism and equality of status.* English and French were made official languages, and the two states were recognised as equal in status (as federated states).
*c) Preservation of institutions.* West Cameroon kept its own legal system (common law), its judiciary, its educational system and local administration, with many powers (for example in local government, education and agriculture) left to the states.
*d) Representation in federal bodies.* The Federal Assembly gave West Cameroon a (smaller) share of seats, but under the Constitution the President and the Vice-President came from different states: Ahidjo was President and Foncha Vice-President, a sign of equality at the top.
*e) Safeguard on constitutional change.* A constitutional amendment required the support of a majority of the deputies of West Cameroon, which in principle protected the federal form.

**3. Ways in which it fell short.**
*a) A strongly centralised federation.* The Federal government kept the most important powers: defence, foreign affairs, currency, finance, the police and security, major economic and development planning, higher education, and the civil service and judiciary at the federal level. A strong President could make decisions with few checks and could legislate by ordinance in certain circumstances, which gave Ahidjo and East Cameroon a dominant role. The Southern Cameroons delegates had wanted greater state powers.
*b) The conditions of the negotiation.* The Foumban Conference lasted only a few days and was held under the Republic's host and chair. The Southern Cameroons delegation, which was not well prepared and divided between Foncha's KNDP and the opposition, saw many of its proposals ignored. Most of the plan for the Constitution was drawn up by the East Cameroon team, and the Southern Cameroons' proposals were only partly accepted.
*c) Population imbalance.* West Cameroon had far fewer people and seats than East Cameroon and could not defend its interests by vote. The safeguard on revision was weak in practice.
*d) Later erosion of the federal system.* The federal government increasingly interfered in West Cameroon's affairs, for example through Federal Inspectors of Administration, the control of economic policies, the merger of parties into one party (the Cameroon National Union, 1966), and the removal of West Cameroon's currency and marketing arrangements. Many Southern Cameroonians felt that they were being assimilated. In 1972 Ahidjo organised a referendum (20 May 1972) abolishing the federation and creating the United Republic of Cameroon, a unitary state, which many Southern Cameroonians opposed. In 1984 the name changed to the Republic of Cameroon. This history has fed the grievances of the "Anglophone problem" later on.

**4. Evaluation.** The Federal Constitution reflected the aspirations of the Southern Cameroonians in form (federation, bilingualism, separate institutions and a Vice-President from West Cameroon), but not to the full extent they wished, since the federal government was strong and the real power lay with the President and the East. In the first years there was some autonomy for West Cameroon, but it was progressively eroded, so that the Constitution reflected their aspirations only to a limited and temporary extent.

**Conclusion.** The Federal Constitution of 1961 met a part of the Southern Cameroonians' aspirations by establishing a federation, official bilingualism and the preservation of some of their institutions, but it gave overwhelming power to the Federal President and the larger East, and its safeguards were weak, so that their hopes of equal partnership and autonomy were largely unfulfilled and the federation was abolished in 1972.
